newsitem.title: BELGIUM: ANTWERP BOURSE, WORLD'S OLDEST, SET TO DISAPPEAR.
newsitem.headline: ANTWERP BOURSE, WORLD'S OLDEST, SET TO DISAPPEAR.

text.p: The Antwerp stock exchange, the world's oldest bourse, is set to disappear when it merges with the Brussels bourse, officials said.

"The Antwerp bourse has done its task. Fundamentally, we are moving in the direction of a merger of the Antwerp bourse into the Brussels bourse," Antwerp bourse chairman Marc Corluy told Reuters. The Antwerp bourse was founded in 1531.
The boards of the two exchanges on Thursday debated several proposals to increase cooperation between the two exchanges.

Brussels bourse deputy director Anne Vleminckx told Reuters its board had given management a mandate to discuss "intense cooperation" between the two exchanges. "Nothing has been signed so far," she said.
But Antwerp bourse officials made no bones about their willingness to be swallowed up by their larger neighbour.

"It makes no economic sense to have two stock exchanges. The idea is that the Antwerp bourse would lose its status as a stock exchange, although our offices and personnel would continue to act as a regional service centre in the coming years," Antwerp bourse director Fonne Hendrickx told Reuters.
He added that he hoped there would be an agreement on a merger by the end of the year.

The Antwerp exchange building was built in 1531 and was the first public building used exclusively for financial and commodity trading. It served as a model for the London exchange building in the late 16th century and for the Amsterdam bourse, which was built in 1611.

The very word "bourse" -- in the sense of a place where traders meet to conduct financial affairs -- originated in Bruges, another northern Belgian town, and spread through Europe via Antwerp in the 16th and 17th centuries.
Variations on the 15th-century Dutch-language word "beurze" now stand for "financial exchange" in most European languages.
Antwerp's 1531 exchange hall still exists, though what little share trading that is left in the port city has moved to modern buildings nearby.

At the end of 1996, total market capitalisation in the few local shares traded on the Antwerp bourse stood at 15 billion francs, just a fraction of the more than 3,000 billion franc capitalisation of the Brussels bourse.
The regional bourses of Ghent and Liege were closed down in a national stock market reform of the early 1990s.
